\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

LLM agents are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks---resolving GitHub issues, debugging production systems, and iterating on multi-file codebases across dozens of editing rounds \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands}.
As these deployments scale, a critical failure mode has emerged that is qualitatively different from crashes or syntax errors: the agent \emph{stagnates}---continuing to produce actions that appear purposeful while making no meaningful progress toward the task goal.
\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} document this degradation on SlopCodeBench, recording verbosity increases of 90\% and quality drops of 80\% in long-horizon coding trajectories, with no agent fully solving any benchmark problem end-to-end.
Crucially, the dominant failure pattern is not simple repetition but what we term \emph{semantic stagnation}: the agent issues varied commands, edits different files, and generates plausible-looking outputs, yet its behavior is functionally stuck.
This ``looks busy but going in circles'' pattern defeats existing monitoring tools, because surface-level action diversity masks the underlying lack of progress.
We observe this phenomenon at scale: across trajectories from two architecturally distinct agents---SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}---on SWE-bench tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, 28.5\% and 6.6\% of sliding windows exhibit stagnation under our silver labeling scheme, respectively, confirming that the failure mode is both prevalent and highly agent-dependent.

Existing approaches address aspects of this problem but fall short in three ways.
First, \emph{repetition detectors} such as cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection} and SpecRA \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop} identify structural repetition---exact or near-exact loops in action sequences---but by design miss semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
Second, \emph{step-level scoring} via process reward models \citep{xi2025agentprm} evaluates individual actions in isolation, discarding the window-level temporal dynamics that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over sequences of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
A sequence of failed commands followed by a strategy switch, for instance, carries different diagnostic information than the same commands evaluated independently.
Third, \emph{LLM self-evaluation} \citep{shinn2023reflexion} is both expensive and fundamentally limited by the stuck model's own judgment; our LLM-as-judge baseline achieves only 0.6625 macro-F1 at \$11.66 per test set, well below lightweight feature-based alternatives.
More fundamentally, none of these approaches asks the prior question: \emph{what signals actually carry stagnation information?}
No systematic study has investigated whether detecting subtle agent failure requires sophisticated semantic understanding or whether simpler structural patterns suffice.

We address this question through a systematic empirical study (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from over 205K windows spanning SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% silver-labeled stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 6.6\% stagnation).
Three labeling functions provide complementary noisy votes: command repetition ($\lambda_1$) targets repetitive behavior, file diff delta ($\lambda_2$) targets output productivity, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) propagates task-level outcomes backward through the trajectory.
Majority vote aggregation produces window-level binary labels with confidence scores.
Our window-level formulation ($k{=}5$ consecutive actions, stride 1) captures short-range temporal patterns---such as repeated failures followed by strategy changes---that step-level approaches cannot express, while providing the granularity to pinpoint \emph{when} stagnation begins and ends within a trajectory, enabling targeted interventions.
Against these silver labels, we systematically compare hand-crafted structural features, a neural embedding probe, and an LLM-as-judge baseline.

Our study yields three principal findings.

\textbf{Finding 1: Stagnation signals are fundamentally structural.}
Thirty hand-crafted features---command repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances---achieve 0.9951 macro-F1 in-domain (Random Forest) and 0.9674 cross-agent macro-F1 (Gradient Boosting, SWE-Agent $\to$ OpenHands), surpassing the GRU embedding probe \citep{cho2014gru} (0.9055 in-domain, 0.751 after full fine-tuning on the target agent) and the LLM-as-judge baseline (0.6625) by wide margins---up to 33.3 percentage points (pp).
We note that in-domain evaluation uses silver labels (\S\ref{sec:circular}); cross-agent transfer and a pending gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}) provide non-circular validation.
The structural advantage is encoder-agnostic: three embedding backbones \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding} all yield probe F1 above 0.90, confirming that the probe's temporal architecture rather than a specific pretrained encoder drives performance.
The in-domain score of 0.9951 reflects circular evaluation---structural features overlap with LF inputs---but the cross-agent score of 0.9674, where models trained on one agent's LF distribution are tested on another with substantially different firing patterns, breaks this circularity.
This finding challenges the prevailing intuition that detecting subtle agent failures requires complex language understanding, and suggests that lightweight structural monitoring---no GPU, under 5\,ms per window---may be more practical than neural or LLM-based approaches for real-time agent oversight.

\textbf{Finding 2: Labeling functions occupy agent-specific temporal niches.}
On SWE-Agent, command repetition ($\lambda_1$) leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps, file diff ($\lambda_2$) is near-concurrent at $-1.20$ steps, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) lags by 6.70 steps.
On OpenHands, $\lambda_1$ reverses from leading to lagging ($+3.32$ steps), where its 92.3\% firing rate produces a 71\% false positive rate on progress windows.
Removing $\lambda_1$ from the OpenHands labeling pipeline improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp, demonstrating that labeling functions validated on one agent architecture can become adversarial on another.

\textbf{Finding 3: Temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote.}
Three temporal label models---time-varying weights (TWV), Hidden Markov Models \citep{safranchik2020linkedhmm}, and lag-aware HMMs---all fail to surpass majority vote on downstream detection.
TWV achieves marginally higher self-evaluated F1 but degrades downstream probe performance by 2.57\,pp.
The root cause: three binary LFs produce too little inter-LF conflict for temporal aggregation to exploit.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Structural signal discovery.} We demonstrate that 30 lightweight structural features achieve near-perfect stagnation detection (0.9951 in-domain, 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1), outperforming neural probes and LLM judges by wide margins (+33.3\,pp over LLM-as-judge), with no GPU and under 5\,ms per window. This redirects agent monitoring from costly representation learning toward lightweight structural approaches.
    \item \textbf{Labeling function temporal dynamics.} We reveal that labeling functions occupy statistically distinct temporal niches relative to stagnation onset, with agent-specific reversals that corrupt silver labels when transferred across architectures, informing future weak-supervision design on sequential agent data.
    \item \textbf{Temporal label model negative finding.} We show that three temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote for downstream detection, despite clear temporal structure in LF firing patterns. This constrains future temporal label model research: the 3-LF regime produces insufficient conflict for temporal aggregation to add value.
\end{enumerate}

## 章节结构（5 个 paragraph-level subsections）

### \section{Related Work} \label{sec:related_work}

**\paragraph{Process Reward Models.}** (~140 words)
- AgentPRM \citep{xi2025agentprm}: step-level rewards for agent trajectories, needs outcome labels + RL pipeline
- PRM framework \citep{choudhury2025prm}: process reward for multi-step reasoning
- ToolPRMBench \citep{li2026toolprmbench}: benchmarking tool-use PRMs
- Trajectory-level RM \citep{fan2026agentrm}: agent reward modeling
- PlanRewardBench \citep{wang2026planrewardbench}: planning reward benchmarks
- DataPRM \citep{qiu2026dataprm}: data-centric PRM
- **对比**：PRMs do step-level scoring needing outcome labels + RL pipelines; we are window-level monitoring via weak supervision, no outcome labels needed at inference time (OB is training-only)

**\paragraph{Agent Self-Reflection and Verification.}** (~120 words)
- Reflexion \citep{shinn2023reflexion}: verbal self-reflection
- LATS \citep{zhou2024lats}: language agent tree search
- ToT \citep{yao2023tot}: tree of thought
- Self-correction limits \citep{huang2024selfcorrect,kamoi2024selfcorrection}: studies showing LLMs struggle to self-correct
- **对比**：these are intervention mechanisms (what to DO when stuck), relying on the stuck model's own judgment; we address the prior detection question (WHEN the agent is stuck), using external structural signals. Our LLM-as-judge baseline (0.6625 F1) illustrates the ceiling of self-evaluation

**\paragraph{Weak Supervision for Sequential Data.}** (~140 words)
- Data programming \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming}: original LF framework
- Snorkel \citep{ratner2017snorkel}: programmatic labeling
- FlyingSquid \citep{fu2020flyingsquid}: efficient label model
- Linked HMM \citep{safranchik2020linkedhmm}: temporal label models for NER (sequential)
- WRENCH \citep{zhang2021wrench}: WS benchmark
- Dawid-Skene \citep{dawid1979em}: EM for annotation
- Multi-resolution sources \citep{sala2019multiresolution}: multi-granularity WS
- **对比**：standard WS assumes i.i.d. samples; Safranchik extends to sequences for NER. We apply WS to agent trajectories (a new domain for WS) and find that temporal extensions (HMM/lag-HMM/TWV) do not help in the low-conflict 3-LF regime—a negative finding that contrasts with Safranchik's positive NER results

**\paragraph{Agent Monitoring and Degradation.}** (~150 words)
- SlopCodeBench \citep{orlanski2026slopcodebench}: coding agent degradation benchmark
- ICLR 2025 monitoring \citep{chen2025monitoring}: sequence-level agent monitoring
- Weak-to-strong monitoring \citep{kale2025weaktostrong}: weak model monitoring strong agents
- Multi-agent failure \citep{cemri2025multiagentfail}: failure patterns in multi-agent systems
- AgentFail \citep{zhu2025agentfail}: agent failure analysis
- **对比**：these works document and motivate the problem; we provide systematic detection study with comparative analysis across signal types (structural vs neural vs LLM)

**\paragraph{Cycle and Anomaly Detection.}** (~150 words)
- CDCS+CDSA cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection}: action-level cycle detection in agents
- SpecRA reasoning loops \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop}: speculative reasoning for loop detection
- TrajAD \citep{liu2026trajad}: trajectory anomaly detection
- **对比**：cycle detectors target structural repetition (exact/near-exact loops), missing semantically diverse stagnation. Our window-level approach with structural features captures BOTH repetitive and non-repetitive stagnation patterns. Our error analysis shows that missed stagnation (85 FN, 64.9% of errors) involves diverse-but-ineffective behavior patterns that repetition detectors would also miss

## 写作指导

- 每个 paragraph 的结构：先简要介绍 related work，最后一两句做 **differentiation**
- 引用格式：行文中 \citet{key}，括号中 \citep{key1,key2}
- 不要对 related work 做负面评价（"fails to" / "poorly"），用中性差异化（"addresses X but not Y" / "operates at step level while we..."）
- 不要重复 Introduction 中已详细说过的数字——简要回指即可（"our LLM-as-judge baseline (\S\ref{sec:main_results})"）

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Process Reward Models.}
Process reward models (PRMs) assign step-level quality scores to guide agent behavior during inference or training.
\citet{xi2025agentprm} introduce AgentPRM, training TD/GAE-based step-level rewards that evaluate both long-term promise and immediate progress in agent trajectories, requiring outcome labels and an RL pipeline.
\citet{choudhury2025prm} formalize the PRM framework and propose InversePRM, learning process rewards from expert demonstrations without outcome labels.
Evaluation benchmarks have emerged in parallel: \citet{li2026toolprmbench} benchmark PRMs on tool-use scenarios, finding that specialized PRMs outperform general-purpose ones, while \citet{wang2026planrewardbench} reveal that all reward model categories---generative, discriminative, and LLM-as-judge---degrade on long-horizon trajectories.
\citet{fan2026agentrm} extend PRMs with structured reasoning traces and multi-dimensional critiques, and \citet{qiu2026dataprm} introduce environment-aware probing for data analysis agents to detect silent errors.
Our work differs in operating at window level rather than step level, requiring no outcome labels or reward annotations at inference time---labeling functions use only observable structural signals---and targeting real-time monitoring ($<$5\,ms per window) rather than training signal generation.

\paragraph{Agent Self-Reflection and Verification.}
Self-reflection methods prompt agents to diagnose and correct their own failures.
\citet{shinn2023reflexion} introduce verbal self-reflection loops, \citet{yao2023tot} propose tree-structured deliberation, and \citet{zhou2024lats} combine Monte Carlo tree search with LLM self-evaluation for language agents.
However, \citet{huang2024selfcorrect} demonstrate that LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without external feedback, and \citet{kamoi2024selfcorrection} confirm that self-correction attempts frequently degrade initial answers.
These methods address what to \emph{do} when an agent is stuck, relying on the stuck model's own judgment for both detection and correction.
We address the prior question---\emph{when} is the agent stuck---using external structural signals rather than self-evaluation.
Our LLM-as-judge baseline (\S\ref{sec:main_results}) illustrates the ceiling of model-based assessment for this detection task.

\paragraph{Weak Supervision for Sequential Data.}
Data programming \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming} enables rapid dataset creation through user-defined labeling functions (LFs), with Snorkel \citep{ratner2017snorkel} operationalizing this into a dependency-aware end-to-end system.
\citet{fu2020flyingsquid} accelerate label model inference via closed-form triplet methods, and \citet{zhang2021wrench} benchmark 22 weak supervision datasets, all assuming i.i.d.\ samples.
Extensions to sequential data relax this assumption: \citet{safranchik2020linkedhmm} introduce a linked HMM for weakly supervised NER, improving over i.i.d.\ label models by incorporating span-level linking rules; \citet{sala2019multiresolution} handle multi-resolution LFs operating at different temporal granularities; and \citet{dawid1979em} provide the foundational EM framework for aggregating noisy annotators, later extended with HMM structure for sequential settings.
We apply data programming to agent trajectories, a novel domain where LFs exhibit systematic temporal dynamics distinct from token-level NER.
Unlike \citeauthor{safranchik2020linkedhmm}'s positive NER results, we find that temporal label models (HMM, lag-HMM, TWV) do not improve over majority vote in our low-conflict 3-LF regime (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models})---a negative result that constrains when sequential extensions to weak supervision add value.

\paragraph{Agent Monitoring and Degradation.}
Recent work documents the prevalence and impact of agent failures at scale.
\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} provide direct evidence of coding agent degradation on SlopCodeBench, recording verbosity increases and quality drops across long-horizon trajectories with no agent fully solving any benchmark task.
\citet{chen2025monitoring} establish that sequence-level context is necessary for effective agent monitoring, as single-step analysis misses failures that emerge only across action sequences.
\citet{kale2025weaktostrong} demonstrate that monitor scaffolding matters more than monitor capability, showing weak models can reliably oversee stronger agents---a finding that motivates lightweight monitoring approaches over scaling up monitor size.
\citet{cemri2025multiagentfail} identify 14 systematic failure modes in multi-agent systems including step repetition as a concrete symptom, and \citet{zhu2025agentfail} show that cascading failures---where single root causes propagate across subsequent decisions---dominate long-horizon tasks.
These works document and motivate the monitoring problem; we complement them with a systematic comparative study across signal types (structural, neural, LLM-based), demonstrating that lightweight structural features suffice for detection and transfer across agent architectures without requiring another LLM or GPU.

\paragraph{Cycle and Anomaly Detection.}
Cycle detection targets structural repetition in agent behavior.
\citet{george2025cycledetection} combine call-stack analysis (CDCS) with embedding similarity (CDSA) to detect action-level cycles in agents, and \citet{pipis2025reasoningloop} analyze reasoning loops in language models using speculative decoding and $n$-gram repetition heuristics.
\citet{liu2026trajad} take a broader view with TrajAD, training a fine-grained verifier through synthetic perturbations to detect trajectory anomalies including task failure, process inefficiency, and unwarranted continuation; they show that general-purpose LLMs perform poorly at zero-shot trajectory verification, motivating specialized approaches.
Cycle detectors are effective for exact or near-exact repetition but by design cannot capture semantically diverse stagnation, where agents vary surface commands while remaining functionally stuck.
Our window-level approach with structural features captures both repetitive and non-repetitive stagnation patterns.
We formulate stagnation as prevalent binary classification over sliding windows rather than rare-event anomaly detection (\S\ref{sec:setup}), and our error analysis (\S\ref{sec:error_analysis}) confirms that the dominant missed-stagnation category involves diverse-but-ineffective behavior---the pattern category that repetition-based detectors would also miss.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic study of progress stagnation detection in LLM coding agents, comparing structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge approaches.
Three findings emerge.

First, stagnation signals are fundamentally structural.
Thirty lightweight features achieve 0.9951 in-domain and 0.9674 cross-agent macro-F1, surpassing neural probes (0.9055) and LLM judges (0.6625) by wide margins.
These features are also data-efficient, maintaining F1 above 0.987 with only 10\% of training data.

Second, labeling functions exhibit agent-specific temporal dynamics.
Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent but reverses on OpenHands, where its high false-positive rate corrupts silver labels---removing it improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp.

Third, temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote.
Three temporal aggregation methods---TWV, HMM, and lag-aware HMM---all underperform majority vote, constrained by insufficient inter-LF conflict among three binary labeling functions.

Agent monitoring should therefore prioritize lightweight structural features ({<}5\,ms per window, no GPU) over embedding or LLM approaches.
The circular evaluation caveat applies to in-domain results; cross-agent transfer provides stronger validation.

Future work includes extending evaluation to non-software-engineering agent domains, online integration with early termination or strategy switching, scaling to {>}10 labeling functions to test whether temporal aggregation becomes useful, and validation against the pending 650-window gold set.

### Table A.1: Encoder Ablation (tab_encoder_ablation)

正文 §5.3 引用为 Appendix Table~\ref{tab:encoder_ablation}。

| Encoder | Dim | Macro-F1 | F1_stag | F1_prog | Best Epoch |

说明文字：All encoders exceed 0.90 macro-F1, confirming the probe's temporal architecture drives performance rather than a specific encoder. BGE-M3 achieves the highest score (+3.6pp over Qwen3), but the gap between encoders (0.5pp) is small relative to the structural--probe gap (8.96pp).

### Table A.2: Window Size Ablation (tab_window_ablation)

正文 §5.3 引用为 Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window_ablation}。

| Window Size (k) | Macro-F1 | F1_stag | F1_prog | Δ vs k=5 |

| 7 | 0.9133 | 0.8791 | 0.9475 | -1.8pp |

说明文字：k=5 is optimal. k=3 lacks sufficient context for stagnation detection (stagnation F1 drops 11.3pp). k=7 dilutes signal by spanning both progress and stagnation phases.
